quote: makes “religion”-associated areas of my brain light up
content: The essay’s conclusion is right, and the reason it is right is a general one the essay does not state. There are no religion-associated areas: neuroimaging of devotional experience finds the reward circuitry (nucleus accumbens, ventromedial prefrontal cortex) and the social-cognition and attention networks that any absorbing, valued experience recruits (Ferguson et al. (2018), on Mormon participants “feeling the Spirit”), and inferring a mental state from activation in a region that many states engage is the reverse-inference fallacy (Poldrack (2006)) that Book III’s annotations discussed. So a shuttle launch and a nativity scene would light up the same regions for the same reason that a football match and a symphony would, and the gloater’s “space travel is your religion” is an inference from a non-specific signal. The essay reaches the right answer by the acid test; the neuroscience reaches it by noting that the premise of the challenge was never evidence of anything.

quote: When someone sets out to write an atheistic hymn—“Hail, oh unintelligent universe,” blah, blah, blah—the result will, without exception, suck.
content: The counterexample is two thousand years old and canonical. Lucretius’s De Rerum Natura is a hymn, in the technical sense (it opens with an invocation and proceeds through praise), to a universe of atoms and void in which the gods do not intervene and death is nothing to us, and it is by common consent one of the great poems of antiquity. Shelley’s “Mont Blanc” and “Queen Mab,” Swinburne’s “Hymn of Man,” Hardy’s “God’s Funeral,” and Stevens’s “Sunday Morning” are all, in the essay’s terms, hymns to the nonexistence of God, and none of them sucks. The essay’s contrast between religious art, “an original expression of emotion,” and atheist art, “imitative,” is also untrue of religious art: the Christian hymn tradition is built on contrafacta, sacred words set to borrowed secular tunes, and the Psalms are formulaic to a degree that has been the subject of form criticism for a century. The claim “without exception” is made from no sample at all, and the first item any sample would contain refutes it.

quote: If God were real, it would destroy the inner uncertainty that brings forth outward fervor in compensation. And if everyone else believed God were real, it would destroy the specialness of being one of the elect.
content: This is a mechanism for religious commitment, and the cognitive science of religion has tested mechanisms; this one is not among the ones that survived. What has support: hyperactive agency detection, the memorability of minimally counterintuitive concepts (Boyer & Ramble (2001)), and costly signalling, in which communes that demand more of their members last longer (Sosis & Bressler (2003)). The essay’s mechanism is Festinger’s When Prophecy Fails generalized, disconfirmation producing compensatory fervour, and Book II’s annotations recorded that the Festinger effect failed to appear in the better-documented cases (Hardyck & Braden (1962)) and that the original Seekers’ proselytizing was brief. Nor does the claim fit the data on religiosity, which is highest where belief is most nearly universal (sub-Saharan Africa, the Islamic world), the opposite of what “the specialness of being one of the elect” predicts. The essay asserts a psychology of believers in order to distinguish itself from them, and the psychology asserted is the one the field abandoned.
